slot.brief: Use the property of definite integrals (f(x)+f(a−x)) to evaluate a definite integral of a trig/algebraic function.

verdicts.working: Set t=2x-1. Then I=\frac14\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{2-t^2}(1+t^2)}\,dt=\frac12\int_0^1\frac{dt}{\sqrt{2-t^2}(1+t^2)}. Using t=\sqrt2\sin\theta and u=\tan\theta, the remaining integral is \int_0^1\frac{du}{1+3u^2}=\frac{\pi}{6\sqrt3}. Thus I=\frac{\pi}{12\sqrt3}.

Substitute u=2x−1: I=(1/4)∫_{-1}^{1}(u+1)/[√(2−u²)(1+u²)]du. Odd part vanishes, so I=(1/2)∫_0^1 du/[√(2−u²)(1+u²)]. With u=√2 sinθ: I=(1/2)∫_0^{π/4} dθ/(1+2sin²θ)=(1/2)∫_0^1 dt/(1+3t²)=(1/2)(1/√3)arctan√3=π/(6√3)≈0.30230, matching numerical integration.

working:
Let $f(x)$ be the integrand. Then $f(x)+f(1-x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2-(2x-1)^2}\,[1+(2x-1)^2]}$, so $I=\dfrac12\int_0^1\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{2-(2x-1)^2}\,[1+(2x-1)^2]}=\dfrac12\int_0^1\dfrac{du}{\sqrt{2-u^2}(1+u^2)}$, using $u=2x-1$ and evenness. With $u=\sqrt2\sin\theta$ and $t=\tan\theta$, $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{du}{\sqrt{2-u^2}(1+u^2)}=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{d\theta}{1+2\sin^2\theta}=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+3t^2}=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}$. Hence $I=\dfrac{\pi}{6\sqrt3}$.

Independent check: Substitute u=2x−1: I=(1/4)∫_{-1}^{1}(u+1)/[√(2−u²)(1+u²)]du. Odd part vanishes, so I=(1/2)∫_0^1 du/[√(2−u²)(1+u²)]. With u=√2 sinθ: I=(1/2)∫_0^{π/4} dθ/(1+2sin²θ)=(1/2)∫_0^1 dt/(1+3t²)=(1/2)(1/√3)arctan√3=π/(6√3)≈0.30230, matching numerical integration.
solution:
Using symmetry under $x\mapsto1-x$,
$$I=\frac12\int_0^1\frac{du}{\sqrt{2-u^2}(1+u^2)},\qquad u=2x-1.
$$Set $u=\sqrt2\sin\theta$, then $t=\tan\theta$; the limits become $0$ to $1$:
$$I=\frac12\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+3t^2}=\frac{\pi}{6\sqrt3}.$$

With $u=\sqrt2\sin\theta$ and $t=\tan\theta$, $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{du}{\sqrt{2-u^2}(1+u^2)}=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{d\theta}{1+2\sin^2\theta}=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+3t^2}=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}$. Hence $I=\dfrac{\pi}{6\sqrt3}$.
